scenario: A developer is building their first agent with the current Microsoft Foundry Agent Service and wants to understand its runtime building blocks before writing code.
question: Which set of components powers stateful, multi-turn interactions in the current Foundry Agent Service?
explanation: D is correct: an agent supplies a reusable model, instructions and tools; a conversation persists input and output items across turns; and a response is one unit of execution that produces output items. B is wrong because threads, messages and runs belong to the classic Agents API (built on the Assistants API pattern), which is deprecated; classic agents retire on March 31, 2027. C is wrong because those are resource and configuration concepts, not runtime conversation objects. A is wrong because those describe building a retrieval index, not an agent conversation.

scenario: An agent needs to analyze an uploaded CSV of sales data, compute statistics, and generate a chart image in response to a user's question.
question: Which built-in Agent Service tool should be enabled?
explanation: C is correct: code interpreter runs Python in a sandbox, so the agent can load the uploaded CSV, compute statistics and generate a chart image. A is wrong because file search retrieves passages from documents; it doesn't execute code. B is wrong because Bing grounding fetches live web results, not calculations over a private file. D is wrong because function calling only invokes functions you define and run yourself, so you would have to build the analysis code.

scenario: A support agent should answer questions strictly grounded in a company's uploaded PDF policy documents, citing the source passages.
question: Which tool is designed for this document-grounded retrieval?
explanation: File search lets you attach a vector store of uploaded documents so the agent automatically retrieves and cites relevant passages when answering — the standard RAG-over-documents tool in Agent Service. Code interpreter executes code, the OpenAPI tool calls external REST APIs, and the Fabric data agent tool queries structured data in Microsoft Fabric — none are document-retrieval tools.

scenario: A developer wants the agent to call their company's internal 'get order status' REST endpoint, deciding on its own when the user's question requires it.
question: Which capability lets the agent invoke a developer-defined function with structured arguments the model decides to populate?
explanation: Function calling lets you register a function's name, description, and JSON-schema parameters; the model decides when to call it and generates the arguments, and your code executes the actual call and returns the result to the agent. Prompt Shields and groundedness detection are safety features, and streaming is about response delivery, not tool invocation.

scenario: A team wants their agent to call an existing internal REST API that already has a published OpenAPI 3.0 specification, without hand-writing a function wrapper for every endpoint.
question: Which Agent Service tool is designed for this?
options: Bing grounding, since it's a general integration tool
Code interpreter, which reimplements the API in Python
File search, by uploading the OpenAPI spec as a document
The OpenAPI tool, which lets the agent call the API directly from its spec
explanation: The OpenAPI tool lets you register an OpenAPI 3.0 specification directly, and the agent can call the described endpoints (with anonymous, API-key, or managed-identity auth) without you writing individual function wrappers. File search would only let the agent read the spec as text, not invoke it; code interpreter and Bing grounding are unrelated to structured API invocation.

scenario: A team building a news-summary agent needs answers that reflect events from earlier today, beyond the model's training cutoff.
question: Which tool grounds the agent's responses in current web content?
explanation: C is correct: the Grounding with Bing Search tool retrieves current web results so the agent can answer time-sensitive questions; the new Foundry Agent Service also offers a generally available web search tool for the same need. B is wrong because file search only retrieves from documents you uploaded. A is wrong because code interpreter executes code and has no live web data. D is wrong because connected agents delegated work to other agents (and aren't available in the new Agent Service); they don't fetch web content.

scenario: An enterprise is moving a classic 'triage' agent to the new Foundry Agent Service. The classic version used the Connected Agents tool to hand work to a 'billing agent' and a 'technical-support agent', each with its own instructions and tools.
question: What does Microsoft recommend for agent-to-agent delegation in the new Agent Service?
options: Expose each specialist as a file search vector store
Keep the Connected Agents tool, which works unchanged in the new API
Merge both specialists into one agent's instructions
Use the A2A tool or a multi-agent workflow
explanation: D is correct: the Connected Agents tool from the classic Agents API isn't available in the new Foundry Agent Service. Microsoft recommends the A2A tool, which calls any A2A-compatible endpoint (including another Foundry agent exposed as an A2A endpoint), or a workflow that orchestrates several Foundry agents declaratively. B is wrong because the migration guide lists Connected Agents as unavailable in the new API. C is wrong because merging the specialists throws away the separate instructions, tools and guardrails that made the split worthwhile. A is wrong because a vector store holds documents for retrieval and can't run another agent.

scenario: A developer notices that after several exchanges, the agent still recalls details from earlier in the conversation without the developer manually resending prior turns.
question: Which Agent Service component is responsible for this persisted conversation history?
explanation: C is correct: a conversation stores items (messages, tool calls and tool outputs) server-side, so each new response can use earlier turns without the client resending them. In the classic API this role was played by a thread. B is wrong because a deployment hosts the model and keeps no conversation state. A is wrong because a connection links the project to an external resource such as Azure AI Search. D is wrong because an evaluation scores outputs after the fact.

scenario: A team wants to build, in its own Python code, a research assistant where planner, researcher and critic agents work over several rounds to refine an answer, with explicit control over the execution path.
question: Which Microsoft framework is designed for this code-first multi-agent orchestration?
explanation: D is correct: Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, built by the same teams. It combines AutoGen's agent abstractions with graph-based workflows that give explicit control over multi-agent execution paths, in Python and .NET. B is wrong because Prompt flow is retiring and was built for chaining LLM steps, not for agents conversing over several rounds. C is wrong because Connected Agents was a classic-only Agent Service tool for simple delegation, and it isn't available in the new Agent Service. A is wrong because Azure AI Search is a retrieval service, not an orchestration framework.

scenario: A .NET team built its agent on Semantic Kernel, exposing existing application functions to the model as plugins, and wants to align with Microsoft's current agent framework for new work.
question: What is the recommended path?
options: Rewrite each plugin as a Prompt flow Python node
Migrate to Microsoft Agent Framework using the Semantic Kernel migration guide
Wrap each plugin as a Connected Agents tool
Stay on Semantic Kernel, because Agent Framework only supports Python
explanation: B is correct: Microsoft describes Agent Framework as the next generation of both Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, and publishes a migration guide from Semantic Kernel. Agent Framework keeps enterprise features such as session-based state, middleware and telemetry, and registers functions as tools. A is wrong because Prompt flow retires on April 20, 2027 and is not an agent framework. C is wrong because the Connected Agents tool delegated to other agents rather than exposing functions, and it isn't available in the new Agent Service. D is wrong because Agent Framework supports .NET and Python, with Go in public preview.

scenario: A team building a RAG-enabled agent chooses to manually construct their retrieval pipeline (outside the File search tool) for finer control over chunking and embeddings.
question: Which two steps are essential when preparing documents for a custom RAG index in Azure AI Search?
options: Compress files and encrypt them with a customer-managed key
Convert all documents to CSV and assign an agent ID
Chunk the documents into passages and generate vector embeddings for each chunk
Fine-tune the base model on the raw document text
explanation: A custom RAG pipeline needs documents split into retrieval-sized chunks and each chunk embedded into a vector representation so the search index can perform vector/hybrid similarity search at query time. Encryption and file format conversion aren't RAG-specific steps, and fine-tuning is a separate technique from retrieval-based grounding.

scenario: A retailer wants an agent that can answer natural-language questions by querying structured sales data already modeled in Microsoft Fabric, without exporting it elsewhere.
question: Which Agent Service tool is designed for this scenario?
explanation: The Fabric data agent tool lets an Agent Service agent query structured data already published in Microsoft Fabric directly, without needing to export or re-index it elsewhere. File search targets unstructured documents, code interpreter executes arbitrary code, and Prompt Shields is a safety feature, not a data-connection tool.

scenario: A support-chat UI needs to display the agent's answer token-by-token as it's generated, rather than waiting for the full response.
question: Which capability should the client application use?
explanation: A is correct: streaming returns partial output as the response is generated, so the UI can render text as it arrives. It changes how the client receives a response, not what the agent produces. B is wrong because batch deployments process large asynchronous jobs at a discount and return results later, the opposite of live delivery. C is wrong because fine-tuning changes model behavior, not delivery timing. D is wrong because content filtering is a safety layer and doesn't control how output is delivered.

scenario: A team wants to change their agent's tone from formal to casual and add a new constraint ('never mention pricing') without redeploying any model or writing new code.
question: What should they update?
options: The Azure region of the deployment
explanation: A is correct: an agent's instructions hold its persona and behavioral rules, so editing them changes tone and adds constraints without retraining or redeploying the model. In the current Agent Service the edit is saved as a new agent version, which you can compare or roll back. B is wrong because fine-tuning is slow and costly and is meant for patterns prompting can't reach, not a tone change. C is wrong because the Azure region affects data processing location and availability, not tone. D is wrong because guardrail blocking levels control harmful-content filtering and can't add a rule such as 'never mention pricing'.

scenario: An architect is deciding whether a customer-support use case needs a single agent with several tools, or a multi-agent design (for example, a Foundry workflow or agents connected through the A2A tool).
question: Which factor most strongly favors a multi-agent design over a single agent with many tools?
options: The task naturally decomposes into distinct specialist roles (e.g., billing vs. technical triage) each needing different instructions, tools, and guardrails
The team wants to minimize the number of API calls at any cost
The use case only ever needs code interpreter
The team has no budget for additional model deployments
explanation: A is correct: multi-agent designs pay off when the problem splits into specialist roles that each need their own instructions, tools and guardrails; a single generalist agent with many tools gets harder to control as its scope grows. B is wrong because adding agents usually adds model calls and hops, so minimizing calls argues for one agent. C is wrong because a use case that needs only code interpreter is a single-tool job with nothing to decompose. D is wrong because each extra agent adds model usage and operating overhead, so a tight budget argues for staying with one agent.

scenario: A team already has a working LangGraph agent with custom orchestration code. They want Foundry to run it with a managed endpoint, automatic scaling and a dedicated Microsoft Entra identity, while keeping their code.
question: Which Foundry Agent Service option fits?
options: An ephemeral agent built by calling the Responses API from their own servers
explanation: A is correct: hosted agents run your own code (for example Agent Framework, LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK), shipped as a container image or a .zip of source code, and Foundry provides the managed endpoint, autoscaling, a dedicated Entra identity and observability. B is wrong because a prompt agent is defined only by configuration (instructions, model and tools), so there is nowhere to put custom orchestration code. C is wrong because a voice-based prompt agent is a managed real-time voice agent, also defined by configuration. D is wrong because an ephemeral Responses API agent runs in the team's own process, so they would host and scale it themselves.

scenario: Twelve agents across three projects each wire up the same MCP servers, OpenAPI tools and web search with their own credentials. Updating a tool means editing every agent.
question: Which Foundry capability is designed to fix this?
options: A toolbox exposed through a single MCP-compatible endpoint
Copying the tool definitions into a shared system prompt
Converting every tool into a function-calling definition
Moving each tool into a file search vector store
explanation: A is correct: a toolbox curates tools once and exposes them through one managed MCP-compatible endpoint, with centralized authentication, guardrails and versioning, so promoting a new toolbox version reaches every consuming agent without code changes. B is wrong because a system prompt can describe tools but can't execute them or hold credentials. C is wrong because function calling runs client-side in each app, so every agent would still carry its own copy. D is wrong because a vector store holds documents for retrieval, not callable tools.

scenario: A product team wants its agent's instructions, tools and model choice to live in the application's source code and go through the same code review as the rest of the app, with no separately managed agent resource in Foundry.
question: Which approach matches this requirement?
options: Create a prompt agent in the Foundry portal and copy its ID into the app
Call the Responses API directly from the app, defining the agent in code
Deploy the agent as a hosted agent container
Store the agent definition as a file in the project's file search vector store
explanation: B is correct: calling the Responses API directly builds an ephemeral agent whose definition lives in application code, so it versions through source control and code review, while still using Foundry models, platform tools and project-level observability. A is wrong because a portal-created prompt agent is a persisted Foundry resource that someone has to keep in sync with the app. C is wrong because a hosted agent is also a separately deployed Foundry resource, aimed at running custom code. D is wrong because a vector store holds documents for retrieval; storing a definition there doesn't make it run.
